cells.tense: You're in it right now, shaping it by hand, and you can feel the shape holding.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you're tending now and write down what done looks like for it, so you can say it's finished and step back, which gives you your hands free again.
cells.core:
You've got something growing on your watch and you're giving it the right amount of yourself — enough to keep it moving, not so much that it won't stand without you. You know where it is and what it needs next, and when a piece of it's finished you can set it down without guilt. That steadiness is rarer than it sounds.

What it hands you is slack. You get to step back and see the whole of it instead of the next chore, and what you've built can go on without your hands on it all the time. This is what's free to feed something else next — the finished thing gets handed over or finally set down, because you can close one out without loosening your grip all the way.
cells.sheetLine: Tending this well looks like knowing when to put it down.
cells.verb: tending what's growing, by hand, for as long as it takes

cells.tense: You're already at a point weeks away, rehearsing how it could all go wrong.
cells.ask: Take the one you've been guarding from other people's eyes and do one finished piece of it out in the open where someone you trust can see it, then eat or rest for ten minutes before you look at it again.
cells.core:
When this is working, the finish line stops moving. You plant, you water, you leave it alone long enough to see what it does — and when a piece is done you can show it without defending it.

Not right now. This week you head off problems before they exist, you hold what's growing tighter than it needs, and you carry it into your sleep. Nothing you tend can settle while you're standing over it, and neither can you. Steadiness here is growth without forcing — care that doesn't exhaust, holding on without clutching. That's not a way to stop caring. It's doing one finished piece where someone can see it, then resting for one stretch that isn't yours to keep working through.

cells.tense: Something you tended didn't make it, and part of you is still standing there saying so.
cells.ask: Start one small living thing — a plant, a batch of dough, a page of notes — in a way that has one step you can finish in a day, and do nothing for it past that step for twenty-four hours.
cells.core:
The know-how is still in you. On a good stretch you take on something small, you give it what it actually asks for, and you let a finished piece stay finished without picking at it.

What's happening instead is this: you know how to tend things — you've done it — but the last good go turned to nothing, and now you stay out of the room rather than start again. What you're holding is care that stopped moving and got filed as a mistake. The plain sense of it comes back when something you take on actually grows. Not by feeling your way into the tired place, but by taking on one small piece you can finish and seeing it finish; doing it is what refills the place that went quiet. What's been shut off can wake up without anything being promised to it.

cells.tense: Someone else is carrying what's growing, and you haven't noticed having a hand in it.
cells.ask: Name out loud, to whoever's nearest, one thing in front of you that only kept going because you kept tending it, and don't follow it with what you could have done better.
cells.core:
When this works, the upkeep is visible on both ends. You tend what you tend, and you can see your own hand in why it's still here — you show up for it, you know what you're holding.

Right now that same work is going on and you call it just how it goes. Routines, a corner of the job, people who'd stall without you — the daily holding is steady and unnamed, and you take its condition for settled fact rather than something you keep up. The steady form here is seeing what you already carry and letting it be known it's carried. Say out loud the one thing only you keep going, and the credit lands where it belongs; the work you've been holding alone gets a witness.

A reader might say their heap is ordinary upkeep with nothing alive in it; each ask is small enough to be worth doing even if that's true.
